{{Short description|Family of probability distributions}}
In [[probability theory]], especially in mathematical [[statistics]], a '''location–scale family''' is a [[indexed family|family]] of [[probability distribution]]s parametrized by a [[location parameter]] and a non-negative [[scale parameter]]. For any [[random variable]] <math> X </math> whose probability distribution function belongs to such a family, the distribution function of <math>Y \,\stackrel{d}{=}\, a + b X</math> also belongs to the family (where <math> \stackrel{d}{=} </math> means "[[Random variable#Equality in distribution|equal in distribution]]"—that is, "has the same distribution as"). 

In other words, a class <math> \Omega </math> of probability distributions is a location–scale family if for all [[cumulative distribution functions]] <math> F \in \Omega </math> and any real numbers <math> a \in \mathbb{R} </math> and <math> b > 0 </math>, the distribution function <math> G(x) = F(a + b x) </math> is also a member of <math> \Omega </math>.

* If <math>X</math> has a [[cumulative distribution function]] <math>F_X(x)= P(X\le x)</math>, then <math>Y= a + b X</math> has a cumulative distribution function <math>F_Y(y) = F_X\left(\frac{y-a}{b}\right)</math>.
* If <math>X</math> is a [[discrete random variable]] with [[probability mass function]] <math>p_X(x)= P(X=x)</math>, then <math>Y= a + b X</math> is a discrete random variable with probability mass function <math>p_Y(y) = p_X\left(\frac{y-a}{b}\right)</math>.
* If <math>X</math> is a [[continuous random variable]] with [[probability density function]] <math>f_X(x)</math>, then <math>Y= a + b X</math> is a continuous random variable with probability density function <math>f_Y(y) = \frac{1}{b}f_X\left(\frac{y-a}{b}\right)</math>.
* If <math>X</math> has a [[moment generating function]] <math>M_X(t)</math>, then <math>Y= a + b X</math> has a moment generating function <math>M_Y(t)=e^{at}M_X(bt)</math>.
* If <math>X</math> has a [[characteristic function (probability theory)|characteristic function]] <math>\varphi_X(t)</math>, then <math>Y= a + b X</math> has a characteristic function <math>\varphi_Y(t)=e^{iat}\varphi_X(bt)</math>.

Moreover, if <math> X </math> and <math> Y </math> are two random variables whose distribution functions are members of the family, and assuming existence of the first two moments and  <math> X </math> has zero mean and unit variance,
then <math> Y </math> can be written as <math> Y \,\stackrel{d}{=}\, \mu_Y + \sigma_Y X </math> , where <math> \mu_Y </math> and <math> \sigma_Y </math> are the mean and standard deviation of <math> Y </math>.

In [[decision theory]], if all alternative distributions available to a decision-maker are in the same location–scale family, and the first two moments are finite,  then a [[Two-moment decision models|two-moment decision model]] can apply, and decision-making can be framed in terms of the [[Expected value|means]] and the [[variance]]s of the distributions.<ref>{{cite journal |last=Meyer |first=Jack |title=Two-Moment Decision Models and Expected Utility Maximization |journal=[[American Economic Review]] |volume=77 |year=1987 |issue=3 |pages=421–430 |jstor=1804104 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last=Mayshar |first=J. |title=A Note on Feldstein's Criticism of Mean-Variance Analysis |journal=[[Review of Economic Studies]] |volume=45 |issue=1 |year=1978 |pages=197–199 |jstor=2297094 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last=Sinn |first=H.-W. |author-link=Hans-Werner Sinn |title=Economic Decisions under Uncertainty |edition=Second English |year=1983 |publisher=North-Holland }}</ref>

== Examples ==

Often, location–scale families are restricted to those where all members have the same functional form. Most location–scale families are [[univariate distribution|univariate]], though not all. Well-known families in which the functional form of the distribution is consistent throughout the family include the following:

* [[Normal distribution]]
* [[Elliptical distribution]]s
* [[Cauchy distribution]]
* [[Uniform distribution (continuous)]]
* [[Uniform distribution (discrete)]]
* [[Logistic distribution]]
* [[Laplace distribution]]
* [[Student's t-distribution#Location-scale t-distribution|Student's t-distribution]]
* [[Generalized extreme value distribution]]

==Converting a single distribution to a location–scale family==
The following shows how to implement a location–scale family in a statistical package or programming environment where only functions for the "standard" version of a distribution are available. It is designed for [[R (programming language)|R]] but should generalize to any language and library.

The example here is of the [[Student's t-distribution|Student's ''t''-distribution]], which is normally provided in R only in its standard form, with a single [[degrees of freedom (statistics)|degrees of freedom]] parameter <code>df</code>. The versions below with <code>_ls</code> appended show how to generalize this to a [[Student's t-distribution#Location-scale t-distribution|generalized Student's t-distribution]] with an arbitrary location parameter <code>m</code> and scale parameter <code>s</code>.

{|
|-
|style="padding-right:10px;"|[[Probability density function]] (PDF):
|style="padding-right:10px;"| <code>dt_ls(x, df, m, s) =</code>
| <code>1/s * dt((x - m) / s, df)</code>
|-
|style="padding-right:10px;"|[[Cumulative distribution function]] (CDF):
|style="padding-right:10px;"| <code>pt_ls(x, df, m, s) =</code>
| <code>pt((x - m) / s, df)</code>
|-
|style="padding-right:10px;"|[[Quantile function]] (inverse CDF):
|style="padding-right:10px;"| <code>qt_ls(prob, df, m, s) =</code>
| <code>qt(prob, df) * s + m</code>
|-
|style="padding-right:10px;"|Generate a [[random variate]]:
|style="padding-right:10px;"| <code>rt_ls(df, m, s) =</code>
| <code>rt(df) * s + m</code>
|}
Note that these generalized functions do not have standard deviation <code>s</code> since standard ''t'' distributions do not have a standard deviation of 1.
